new_statements.rule_in_words: The phonology summary lists 'Stress' as a phonological unit of Northern Kankanay (alongside the consonant and vowel inventories), i.e. the language has word stress that Reid/Hettick treat as a phonemic feature; nothing is said about where it falls, whether it is predictable, or about secondary stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Reid 1971 entry 24 describes the dialect of Balugan, Sagada, Mountain Province ('also referred to as Sagada Igorot, or Western Bontoc'), data from Donna Hettick 1966. Vanoverbergh 1917 (not opened) describes 'Lepanto Igorot as it is spoken at Bauco' (Bauko, Mountain Province), a different Northern Kankanay locality. The listed archive.org URL for Reid 1971 is actually the Ilongot (ilk) excerpt, not Northern Kankanay.

new_statements.quote: ACCENT. Although some rules for accent could be made, it is deemed useless, as there would be too many exceptions, and the rules made for other Filipino dialects are about the same as those that could be made for Lepanto-Igorot. In general, however, a suffix draws the accent after it, although there are many exceptions. EXAMPLES From kayáyung: kayayúngen. To scratch. ... From pili: pilien. To choose. From bilí: bilién. To examine. ... EXCEPTIONS From tontón: tontónen. To ascertain. From bang-óg: bang-ógan. To cudgel. ... NOTES 1. When the stem consists of only one syllable the accent may generally be put on the prefixes ma, na, and ka, provided there be no suffix. ... 3. Sometimes, when a reduplication of the stem occurs, the accent is transferred from the last syllable but one to the last. EXAMPLES láki and laklakí

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Kankanay, Northern has an empty rule and there are no existing statements, so nothing to agree or conflict with; this 1917 primary description supplies the first statement: accent is lexically placed (penult or final, marked per word, no rule 'because too many exceptions'), with morphologically conditioned rightward shift under suffixation. Compatible with the usual Philippine/Cordilleran contrastive-stress profile.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Vanoverbergh declines to state a placement rule for word accent because any rule would have 'too many exceptions' (i.e. accent position is not predictable and must be learned per word, as in 'other Filipino dialects'); accent is marked with an acute on every cited form throughout the grammar, and the examples show both penultimate (págew? e.g. ágew, láki, píli) and final (bilí, tontón, dengdéng, sap-éy) accent on stems. The only generalisations offered are morphological: a suffix ordinarily pulls the accent one syllable rightward (kayáyung -> kayayúngen), with listed exceptions where it stays (tontón -> tontónen); monosyllabic stems may throw the accent onto prefixes ma-/na-/ka- (náet ~ naét); the affix -an-/-um-an- can move accent to a preceding syllable; reduplication sometimes shifts accent from penult to final (láki ~ laklakí); superlative suffixes -gan/-yan etc. draw the accent onto the vowel immediately preceding the suffix consonant (p. ~356).
new_statements.exceptions: Explicit list of exceptions to suffix-induced accent shift (tontónen, bang-ógan, adáden?, natildían); optional accent on prefixes ma/na/ka with monosyllabic stems; accent retraction with -an-/kuman- 'prolonged sound' forms; penult-to-final shift under reduplication. Also notes (p. 341) that e is mute except in open accented syllables, and (Introduction, p. 337) that the description is strictly of Bauco speech, pronunciation differing even in settlements half an hour away.
new_statements.identity_note: Vanoverbergh describes 'Lepanto Igorot as it is spoken at Bauco' (Bauko, Mountain Province) and stresses (p. 337) that the grammar covers Bauco speech only, pronunciation differing even in nearby settlements (e.g. s pronounced as aspirated h at Bauco but not in many other Lepanto-Igorot towns, p. 342). Bauko Kankanaey is conventionally assigned to Northern Kankanay (nort2877), matching the item.

This phonemic inventory was inherited intact by Proto-Bontok-Kankanaey (PBK), although the back vowel is usually represented by o, its most common phonetic manifestation in current dialects.
